title: Information & data for decision-making
blurb: Explain why projects must produce information and collect data to make decisions and communicate them, and walk the information management process in order.
question: A water company's pipe-replacement project keeps survey data on engineers' laptops, in emails and in three spreadsheets. The board then prioritises streets using out-of-date figures. Why does information management matter, and what process should the project follow?

teach.body: Data are raw facts: dates, costs, survey readings. Information is data processed and organised so it means something to the person using it. Projects need timely, accurate, relevant information to make good decisions, and records to communicate those decisions and actions to stakeholders, giving transparency and an audit trail. The information management process has six stages: collection, storage, curation, dissemination, archiving and destruction. In plain English: gather it, keep it safe, keep it right, share it, file it, then dispose of it properly.

steps.label: Storage
steps.sub: Keep it secure, accessible and backed up

steps.label: Curation
steps.sub: Check, organise, version and maintain it

steps.label: Dissemination
steps.sub: Share the right information with the right people

steps.label: Archiving
steps.sub: Retain records for audit and lessons

teach.caption: Memory hook: 'Cats Sleep Comfortably During Afternoon Downpours'.

teach.h: What goes wrong if a stage is done badly
head: Stage
If it is done badly
rows: Gaps or unreliable data feed bad decisions
Data lost, insecure or impossible to find
People act without knowing the decision
No audit trail; lessons are lost
Kept too long: legal and privacy risk

teach.body: Good information is timely (there when the decision is made), accurate (checked, from reliable sources), relevant (what this audience needs, no more), complete enough to decide on, and secure. Projects aim for a single source of truth under version control, so the board, team and suppliers all look at the same figures. Recording decisions and their reasons, for example in a decision log, lets stakeholders see what was decided, by whom and why.

teach.h: From data to decision to action
teach.caption: Information does two jobs: it informs the decision, then it communicates the decision and the actions that follow.

teach.text: Order traps: curation comes BEFORE dissemination (check it, then share it), and archiving comes BEFORE destruction. Archiving is not deleting: archived records are kept and retrievable for audit and lessons. Destruction happens only when the retention period ends, and must be secure, especially for personal data under data protection law.

teach.h: Information in linear and iterative projects
Scenario: Severn Valley Water's mains renewal
teach.body: Survey crews once kept pipe data on laptops and in three spreadsheets, and the board prioritised streets using last year's figures. Now crews record readings in one app (collection); data sits in a single access-controlled repository (storage); a data officer removes duplicates and controls versions (curation); the board gets a weekly dashboard and residents get street notices (dissemination); as-built records pass to the asset team (archiving); and residents' contact details are securely deleted when the retention period ends (destruction).

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: State why information matters: it informs decisions and communicates actions and decisions to stakeholders.
Name the six stages in order, with a short explanation of each if the marks allow.
Give the qualities of good information: timely, accurate, relevant.
Mention transparency and an audit trail, for example a decision log.
Apply it to the scenario: who needs which information, and when.
Data are raw facts; information is data organised to give meaning for a decision.
Information informs decisions and communicates actions and decisions to stakeholders.
Process, in order: collection, storage, curation, dissemination, archiving, destruction.
Good information is timely, accurate and relevant, from a single version-controlled source.
Archive first; destroy securely only when the retention period ends.

summary: You can now explain why projects produce information and collect data: to inform decisions and to communicate actions and decisions with a clear audit trail. You can also put the six stages of information management in order and say what goes wrong when each is neglected.

A.q: Which shows the stages of the information management process in the correct order?
options: Collection, storage, curation, dissemination, archiving, destruction
Collection, curation, storage, archiving, dissemination, destruction
Storage, collection, curation, dissemination, destruction, archiving
Collection, storage, dissemination, curation, archiving, destruction
A.why: The order is collection, storage, curation, dissemination, archiving, destruction: gather it, keep it, check it, share it, file it, dispose of it.

whyNot.1: Storage comes before curation, and dissemination comes before archiving.
whyNot.2: Collection comes first, and archiving comes before destruction.
whyNot.3: Curation (checking and organising) comes before dissemination.

A.q: Which stage of information management involves checking, organising and maintaining information so it stays accurate and usable?
options: Dissemination
Archiving
Collection
Curation
A.why: Curation keeps information accurate, organised, current and version-controlled so it can be trusted.

whyNot.0: Dissemination is sharing information with the people who need it.
whyNot.1: Archiving retains records after they are no longer in active use.
whyNot.2: Collection is gathering the data in the first place.

A.q: Why is producing good information important on a project?
options: It removes the need for a project sponsor
It replaces stakeholder meetings
It informs and communicates decisions
It guarantees the project's benefits
A.why: Information lets decision-makers choose well, and it communicates the resulting actions and decisions to stakeholders.

whyNot.0: The sponsor's role remains; information supports their decisions.
whyNot.1: Information supports engagement but does not replace talking to stakeholders.
whyNot.3: Good information improves decisions but cannot guarantee benefits.

B.q: A board prioritised streets using last year's survey spreadsheet, although newer readings existed elsewhere. Which stage of information management failed most clearly?
options: Destruction: data was deleted too soon
Curation: versions were not controlled
Archiving: records were stored offsite
Collection: too many surveys were done
B.why: Curation keeps information checked, current and version-controlled. Here old and new data existed side by side and the wrong version was used.

whyNot.0: Nothing was deleted; the problem was an outdated version being used.
whyNot.2: Archived records are not in active use; the board used a live but outdated file.
whyNot.3: More surveys did not cause the problem; uncontrolled versions did.

B.q: After a marketing project closes, the customer contact data it collected is kept indefinitely 'just in case'. Which stage has been neglected?
options: Destruction
Dissemination
Collection
Curation
B.why: Information should be securely destroyed when its retention period ends. Keeping personal data indefinitely creates legal and privacy risk.

whyNot.1: Dissemination is about sharing information, not disposing of it.
whyNot.2: The data was collected; the problem is what happened after closure.
whyNot.3: Curation maintains active information; this is about disposal at the end of its life.

B.q: What is the main purpose of archiving project information at closure?
options: To delete data that is no longer needed
To send final updates to stakeholders
To capture new data from the users
To keep records for audit and learning
B.why: Archiving retains records in a retrievable form so they can support audits, future reference and lessons learned.

whyNot.0: Deleting data is destruction, which comes after archiving and only when retention ends.

C.q: An iterative team relies on a visible task board and a backlog rather than lengthy documents. Which statement is still true?
options: Records can be thrown away after each time box
Only the product owner may see information
Information still needs managing and archiving
Decisions no longer need to be communicated
C.why: Iterative projects use lighter documentation, but information must still be stored, curated, shared, archived and eventually destroyed properly.

whyNot.0: Records are still needed for audit, lessons and handover.
whyNot.1: Iterative working relies on transparency; information is shared widely.
whyNot.3: Communicating decisions is just as important, often more frequent.

C.q: A sponsor asks why the project manager records each key decision, who made it and why, in a decision log. What is the best reason?
options: It lets the PM avoid escalating issues
It gives an audit trail and transparency
It replaces the need for progress reports
It is needed only for legal disputes
C.why: A decision log shows what was decided, by whom and why: an audit trail that keeps stakeholders informed and supports accountability.

whyNot.0: Recording decisions does not remove the need to escalate.
whyNot.2: Progress reports are still needed; the log complements them.
whyNot.3: It supports governance and learning every day, not just in disputes.

C.q: Which TWO qualities of information most support good project decisions? (1) timely (2) as voluminous as possible (3) relevant to the decision (4) unverified but fast
options: 1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
1 and 3
C.why: Information needs to arrive in time and be relevant to the decision (and accurate). Volume and speed without checking do not help.

whyNot.0: Item 2 is wrong: too much information hides what matters.
whyNot.1: Both are wrong: volume and unverified speed undermine decisions.
whyNot.2: Item 4 is wrong: unverified information may be inaccurate.

reteach.title: Think of a public library
reteach.question: How does a library handle its books from the day they arrive to the day they are disposed of, and how does that mirror project information?

blocks.body: A library acquires books (collection), shelves them securely in the right place (storage), catalogues and repairs them and replaces out-of-date editions (curation), and lends them to readers who need them (dissemination). Rarely used but important volumes move to the archive stacks (archiving). Damaged duplicates are eventually pulped (destruction). Skip the cataloguing and a reader borrows the 2009 tax guide: the library version of deciding on out-of-date data.

blocks.text: A library never pulps a book before deciding whether to archive it. The same goes for projects: archive first, and destroy only when the retention period ends.

explain.body: Data are raw facts; information is data organised to give meaning. Information does two jobs: it informs decisions, and it communicates the actions and decisions to stakeholders.

test.q: What is the difference between data and information?
options: Data is always digital; information is on paper
Information is data organised to give meaning
Data is checked; information is unchecked
Information is only produced at closure
test.why: Data are raw facts; information is data processed and organised so it is meaningful for a purpose.

whyNot.0: Both data and information can be digital or on paper.
whyNot.2: Checking belongs to curation and applies to both.
whyNot.3: Information is produced throughout the project.

explain.body: Collect data from reliable sources in a consistent way, then store it securely, backed up and accessible to those who need it: ideally one repository, not scattered laptops and inboxes.

test.q: Survey readings on a project are kept on individual engineers' laptops. Which stage of information management is weakest?
options: Dissemination
Destruction
Storage
Archiving
test.why: Storage should be secure, backed up and accessible. Data scattered on laptops can be lost and is hard for others to find.

whyNot.0: Sharing suffers as a result, but the root weakness is where the data is kept.
whyNot.1: Nothing is being disposed of here.
whyNot.3: This is live data, not closed records.

explain.body: Curation checks, organises and version-controls information so it can be trusted. Only then is it disseminated: the right information, to the right people, in the right format, at the right time.

test.q: Why must curation happen before dissemination?
options: So only checked, current data is shared
So data can be deleted before sharing
So stakeholders can curate it themselves
So archiving can be skipped at closure
test.why: Curation makes sure information is accurate and current before anyone relies on it.

whyNot.1: Deletion is destruction, the final stage.
whyNot.2: Curation is the project's job; stakeholders should receive trustworthy information.
whyNot.3: Archiving is still required at closure.

explain.body: At closure, records are archived so they remain retrievable for audit and lessons. When the retention period ends, they are destroyed securely, which matters most for personal and commercially sensitive data.

test.q: Which statement about archiving and destruction is correct?
options: Destruction comes first, followed by archiving
Archived records are deleted at closure
Both are skipped on iterative projects
Archive first; destroy when retention ends
test.why: Records are archived at closure and destroyed securely only once their retention period has ended.

whyNot.0: The order is the other way round: archiving, then destruction.
whyNot.1: Archived records are kept, not deleted at closure.
whyNot.2: Iterative projects still archive and dispose of information properly.
